title: Complexe de De Rham à puissance divisée [conférence de 1976 à l’IHÉS] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This is page 'EZ 3' of a sequence on the Eilenberg–Zilber theorem, inserted into the 1976 IHES lecture notes on the divided-power de Rham complex. The aim is to set up Steenrod-type (E-infinity / homotopy-commutativity) structure on simplicial chains. The next page then defines P f, D_i and the Steenrod powers P^i via K(Z/p,1).

(1) Strict facts. The shuffle (Eilenberg–Zilber) map ∇: N(A)⊗N(B) → N(A⊗B) and the Alexander–Whitney map AW: N(A⊗B) → N(A)⊗N(B) are both associative. The shuffle map is strictly graded (anti)commutative. AW is commutative only up to homotopy.

(2) Diagrammatic formulation, with reference to Illusie's thesis (Complexe cotangent et déformations, the chapter on multisimplicial objects and totalisation). Take a trisimplicial object X_{***}. Normalising gives a triple complex; totalising in directions 1 and 2 (∫_{12}) and then totalising again gives a complex. Alternatively, take the diagonal Δ_{12} to get a bisimplicial object, then normalise and totalise. Eilenberg–Zilber gives comparison maps between these routes. Associativity amounts to compatibility of the resulting squares. 'Clair pour ZX': for the free simplicial abelian group Z[X] everything is explicit.

(3) Commutativity statement. Let X be a simplicial set. Consider the Hom-complex Hom^•(Z(X×X)~, Z X~ ⊗ Z X~), using normalised/reduced chains. It carries a Σ_2-action by swapping factors on both sides. It has an augmentation to Z, read off in degree 0 at the level of X_0×X_0 → X_0⊗X_0, or by restricting to X → pt. One should really pass to the functorial version Hom(Z(−×−), Z(−)⊗Z(−)) → Z: the complex of natural transformations as X varies.

(4) Theorem attributed to Dold ('Über die Steenrodschen Kohomologieoperationen', Annals 1961). The complex of natural transformations Hom^•(Z(X^n), ZX^{⊗n}), and likewise the reverse direction Hom^•(ZX^{⊗n}, Z(X^n)), is a free resolution of Z in Σ_n-modules.
- Acyclicity comes from acyclic models / representability: Z(X^n)_k is represented by n disjoint copies of Δ^k.
- Freeness comes from Σ_n permuting those copies.
- Consequently any such complex can play the role of W_n = Z EΣ_n from the previous page. This gives Σ_n-equivariant maps W_n ⊗ Z(X^n) → ZX^{⊗n} that lift AW and encode its higher homotopy-commutativity.

(5) 'On bricole pour avoir un complexe de chaînes': the Hom^• complex is unbounded in both directions (cochain-like), so one truncates or regrades to get a non-negative chain complex resolution. This feeds the next page's construction P f = μ∘f^{⊗p}∘λ and the reindexing D_i ↦ P^i, which yields the Cartan formula.
errors: The text says 'Pour tout X, ce complexe ... est une résolution libre'. This is misleading. For a fixed X the Hom complex is not a free Σ_n-resolution of Z. The correct statement, added by Grothendieck himself ('pour X variable'), concerns the complex of natural transformations between the functors X ↦ Z(X^n) and X ↦ ZX^{⊗n}.
The Hom^• complex is unbounded and needs truncation or regrading to be a resolution in the usual sense. Grothendieck flags this ('On bricole') but leaves the gap unfilled.

deep.surprise_reason: These are lecture-preparation notes summarising classical material: Eilenberg–Zilber, Illusie's multisimplicial formalism, and Dold's acyclic-models construction of Steenrod operations. The idea of the natural-transformation complex as a free Σ_n-resolution (essentially the Eilenberg–Zilber E-infinity operad) is well documented later. Its appearance in a divided-power de Rham context is mildly interesting historically, but the page contains nothing new.
transcription_corrections: Dold's paper title is 'Über die Steenrodschen Kohomologieoperationen' (Ann. of Math. 73, 1961); the page abbreviates it as 'Über Steenrodsche Operationen ...'.
'Hom'' in the image should be read as Hom^• (graded Hom complex), with tildes denoting normalised/reduced chains: Hom^•(Z(X×X)~, Z X~ ⊗ Z X~) → Z.
Line 'On peut exprimer ceci avec des diagrammes d'objets {multi/tri}simpliciaux' — the diagram involves trisimplicial X_{***}, so 'multisimpliciaux' fits better than 'bisimpliciaux'.
